topics.title: Privacy and data
topics.summary: Identifiable student work must not be shared with public AI tools, including personal paid accounts. University-SSO Copilot has a separate enterprise-protection context.
topics.scope: September 2026 teaching guidance; the replacement Acceptable Use Guideline PDF remains unavailable, so its full data-class rules are not asserted.

claims.text: Identifiable student work must not be shared with public AI tools, including personal paid accounts. University-SSO Copilot has a separate enterprise-protection context.

evidence.quote: Privacy and Data security : Student work that can identify, or reasonably be linked to, an individual student is personal information under Ontario's Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA) and must be handled accordingly.  Information Security's Artificial Intelligence Acceptable Use Guideline  (May 2026) notes that identifiable student work is confidential information and cannot be shared in public AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini), whether the account is free or a paid personal one. Prompts in those tools have left the University's custody and may train someone's next model. If a teaching/assessment task needs an external tool, you should strip the prompt of any identifying information, ask Information Security to review the tool (if not previously reviewed;  infosec@uoguelph.ca ), or build the task so students enter their own work themselves (while offering them an opt-out).
evidence.title: Teaching and learning with generative AI this fall — Sep 3, 2026 OTL memo

claims.text: Identifiable student work must not be shared with public AI tools, including personal paid accounts. University-SSO Copilot has a separate enterprise-protection context.

evidence.quote: Microsoft Copilot, signed in with your University single sign-on, can be used for student information. Authenticated Copilot runs inside the University's Microsoft environment with enterprise data protection ( Copilot: Get Started ). Faculty and staff use various tools for other purposes, such as drafting, brainstorming, summarizing public material, and that is fine; but do not share student information with third-party tools. For more information, please review the  Information Security guidelines for differentiation among data types .

claims.text: Submitting AI-completed material without instructor permission may constitute academic misconduct. AI detection tools are not approved to support an integrity allegation.

evidence.quote: Academic Integrity : Ensuring students are learning with integrity can be challenging in the age of AI. The calendar's  existing academic misconduct provisions  (Unauthorized Aids and Assistance) cover unauthorized use of AI. Being explicit about your expectations regarding AI use in individual assessments and having students declare sources and prompts for AI use can be helpful promoting a culture of integrity. Use of  tools for detecting AI  use are not approved at Guelph and cannot be used to support an allegation of a breach of academic integrity. Continue to talk with your students and consider ways of re-designing assessments that maximize learning while minimizing opportunities for integrity breaches. This  question guide  may be helpful for engaging in those conversations regarding suspected misuse of Generative AI.
evidence.title: Teaching and learning with generative AI this fall — Sep 3, 2026 OTL memo
